afrikaans-af.ambiguities: As in Dutch, hiatus is marked by diaeresis (reël, knieë, koeël, poësie), so false vowel digraphs are rare; the diaeresis forms eë/ieë/oeë are vowel + separate ë. sk is s+k (skool), never a digraph. ng across boundaries (aangee, ingaan). Circumflex forms (sê, wêreld, môre, rûe, wîe) are single letters plus e: ôe/ûe/îe spell two syllables (/oːə/), not one phoneme, so they are not listed.

multigraphs.note: used to write plosive /ɡ/ in loans (gholf, ghoeroe)
loans and names only (chirurg, Christus); native /x/ is g

afrikaans-af.notes: Afrikaans spelling is largely Dutch-based and quite transparent; Dutch ch/sch were replaced by g/sk. English loan spellings (sh, th, ch) occur in the Wikipedia corpus.

albanian-sq.ambiguities: Essentially none: the nine digraphs are letters of the 36-letter alphabet, and sequences such as s+h, d+h, n+j, g+j, z+h, x+h do not occur across morpheme boundaries in standard spelling (compounds are rare and hyphenated). ll/rr are never l+l/r+r. Other doubled letters do not occur except in a few loans/compounds (e.g. 'për-rreth' is written with hyphen or as rr).

multigraphs.note: letter of the alphabet, contrasts with l /l/
letter of the alphabet, trill, contrasts with r /ɾ/

albanian-sq.notes: Standard Albanian (1972 Congress of Orthography) is highly transparent; ë is /ə/ (often silent word-finally), ç /t͡ʃ/, x /d͡z/, q /c/, y /y/ are single letters. The alphabet column lacks w (loans only).

amharic-am.notes: Syllabary: each fidel is one consonant-plus-vowel grapheme.

arabic-ar.notes: Unpointed Modern Standard Arabic: every consonant is one letter; ا و ي double as long-vowel letters /aː uː iː/; the hamza forms أ إ آ ؤ ئ ء are single letters for /ʔ/ (+ vowel seat); ة (ta marbuta) and ى (alif maqsura) are word-final allographs. Short vowels and shadda (gemination) are not written, so a doubled letter in the data is always two phonemes across a morpheme boundary (ممكن, اللغة with the article ال-). The definite article ال assimilates to sun letters (الشمس /aʃʃams/) but is still spelled letter by letter. No digraphs.

aragonese-an.ambiguities: Several competing orthographies exist (Uesca 1987 with ñ/z/x; SLA 2004; Academia de l'Aragonés 2010 with ny/tz/ix; Academia Aragonesa de la Lengua 2023, close to 2010 but cu for /kw/, optional ny/ñ, no final tz). The corpus (Aragonese Wikipedia-type text) follows the 2010 norm (ny 162 types vs ñ 5; tz 106; ix 318), which is described here; a few Uesca-norm or Spanish items (español, cañada, cuando) are mixed in. ix: exclude the few learned words where x = /ks/ after i (e.g. 'fixar'? not attested; galaxia is a+x). qu/gu need the before-e/i restriction (quan, qual, augua, igual). tz is word-final only; y between vowels (yo, mayor) is a consonant /ʝ/, word-final y in ai/ei/oi diphthongs (rei? 'rei' written with i). Diphthongs (ie, ue, ua, ai, ei, oi, au, eu, ou) are glide + vowel and not listed.

multigraphs.note: chugar, mesache, cheneral, marcha (also the reflex of etymological /dʒ/)
anyo, sinyor, companyero (Academia de l'Aragonés 2010 / AAL 2023 spelling); the Uesca-1987 spelling ñ occurs in only 5 corpus types

word-final 2nd-plural verb endings and plurals in the 2010 norm (totz, fetz, puetz, esperatz): /ts/ in Benasque/Ribagorçan, /θ/ elsewhere; written -z in Uesca-1987 and in the AAL 2023 norm

aragonese-an.notes: Low-resource standardisation; the 2010 Academia de l'Aragonés 'Propuesta ortográfica' is the dominant system in the corpus. Doubled letters other than ll/rr are rare and two phonemes. No ü in the stripped alphabet, so gü/qü cannot occur. Phoneme values follow the Wikipedia orthography table; dialectal variation (ix /jʃ/, tz /ts/) is noted but grapheme boundaries are stable. Context rule applied: qu/gu count as one grapheme only before e/i (que, guerra); before a/o the u is a vowel letter (cuando, agua).

armenian-hy.ambiguities: ու is unambiguous: ո+ւ never spells anything else. ո and ե are single letters that spell /vo/ and /je/ word-initially (ոչ, երեք) and /o/ /e/ elsewhere; և is a single character in alphabets.tsv and spells /jev/ or /ev/ – both are one-letter/two-phoneme cases the tool cannot express. Doubled letters are real geminates (mostly -ն + definite article -ն: բանն, անունն; loanwords), i.e. two phonemes.

multigraphs.note: the only spelling of /u/ in Eastern Armenian; ւ never stands alone except in եւ

EXCEPTION: decomposed spelling of the ligature և (1,299 word types in the corpus use եւ, 567 use և): /jev/ word-initially (եւ 'and'), /ev/ elsewhere (բարեւ, նաեւ). Two phonemes, listed because ւ never occurs outside ու/եւ; drop if strictly one-phoneme graphemes are required.

armenian-hy.notes: Eastern Armenian, reformed (Soviet) orthography as used on hy.wikipedia. Apart from ու and the ligature և/եւ the script is one letter = one phoneme. ը is sometimes left unwritten word-internally (schwa epenthesis) but that does not create multigraphs.

assamese-as.notes: Abugida: each consonant letter and each vowel sign (or the inherent vowel) is one grapheme, so the graphemic level equals the orthographic (akshara-based) one.

asturian-ast.ambiguities: gu/qu need the before-e/i restriction (agua, llingua, cuatro). ḷḷ is a doubled letter under the tool's generic rule anyway, so listing it only fixes the class/phoneme. ḥ (/h/, Eastern Asturian ḥacer, guaḥe) is a single letter and is fine. Dialectal yy (/ɟ͡ʝ/, Western) and ts (/ts/, Western; 'ts' in tsar) are not listed: yy is covered by the doubles rule and ts is almost always t+s (plurals/loans). x is a single letter /ʃ/ (xente, dixo; /ks/ in learned words: esperiencia is spelt without x). Diphthongs (ie, ue, ua, ai, ei, oi, au, eu, ou, iu) are glide + vowel and not listed; ei/ou are true falling diphthongs in Western Asturian but the standard (Central) has e/o. ñ is a single letter /ɲ/.

multigraphs.note: llingua, lleche, castiellu; never a doubled l

asturian-ast.notes: Academia de la Llingua Asturiana norms (Normes ortográfiques, 1981, 7th ed. 2012). Doubled letters other than ll/rr/ḷḷ are two phonemes (acción, innovación) and rare. Corpus contains ḥ (16 types, loans like ḥawaianu, suaḥili) and ḷḷ (2 types) — both marginal. Context rule applied: qu/gu count as one grapheme only before e/i (que, guerra); before a/o the u is a vowel letter (cuando, agua).

azerbaijani-az.ambiguities: As in Turkish, doubled vowels in loans (saat, maaş, təəssüf) are two syllables and would be wrongly merged by the doubling rule; doubled consonants are geminates. The letter sequence ts (414 types) is t+s across morpheme boundaries (etsin), not a digraph.
azerbaijani-az.notes: Latin alphabet of 1991/1992: one letter = one phoneme; x = /x/, q = /ɡ/, ğ = /ɣ/, ə = /æ/, c = /dʒ/, ç = /tʃ/, ş = /ʃ/, j = /ʒ/ are single letters. The apostrophe used until 2004 for the glottal stop (mə'na) is not in the alphabet and is absent from the data.

balinese-ban.ambiguities: ngg = ng+g (tunggil, inggih, kaanggén) and the rare ngh are correctly handled left-to-right. Doubled vowels are two syllables (kaanggén = ka+anggén); doubled consonants arise only at morpheme boundaries (nn in -nyané after n-final stems is n+ny). Vowel sequences ai/au (kain, rai, rauh, laut) are separate syllables in native Balinese; Indonesian diphthongs appear only in loans (partai, danau) and are not listed.
balinese-ban.notes: Latin spelling ('EyD Bali Latin', 1974, following Indonesian EYD): 26 letters plus the diacritic é to distinguish /e/ from e = /ə/; word-final /ə/ is written a. Loan sounds /f kh q sy v z x/ exist only in Indonesian/Arabic loans (khas, makhluk, masyarakat, syair) and were not listed; Sanskrit/Old Javanese spellings dh, th (dharma, artha, tirtha) are etymological, not Balinese digraphs (Balinese has no retroflex contrast in the standard spelling). The corpus writes é consistently (sané, désa, nénten).

banjar-bjn.ambiguities: ai/au: identical problem to Malay — about half of the corpus occurrences are vowel sequences before a consonant or across a prefix boundary (ba-isi, ma-ulah, sa-urang) and would be mis-tokenised; /ui/ was not listed because nearly all corpus ui tokens are u + the suffix -i (malalui, diakui, ditamui). nn = n + ny in lainnya, buhannya; doubled vowels are two syllables (kaadaan). Pre-1972 spellings (soedah, itoe, radja, djoea) occur in a few corpus types.

multigraphs.note: listed as a single letter of the standard alphabet (Hapip 2006; Pedoman Umum Ejaan Bahasa Banjar 2009): nang, ngini, urang, ngaran
single letter of the standard alphabet: inya, banyu, hanyar, manyambat
Wikipedia (Durasid): 'the diphthongs are /ai/, /au/, /ui/'; as in Malay, only in open syllables (sabagai, sampai, sungai, dipakai); two syllables in baisi, lain
open syllables only (pulau, atau, walaupun); two syllables in laut, daun, maulah (ma+ulah)

banjar-bjn.notes: Banjar (Malayic) uses Indonesian-style spelling; the standard alphabet is a b c d é g h i j k l m n ny ng o p r s t u w y, with é = /ɛ/ (Hulu dialect); loan letters f q v x z only in Indonesian loans. Vowel inventory is disputed (3 vs 5 monophthongs); no standard schwa. kh/sy/gh in the corpus (khas, akhir, masyarakat, panghulu = ng+h) are Indonesian/Arabic loan spellings and were not listed. Confidence is low mainly for the diphthongs. Decision: the diphthong spellings (ai, au) count as one grapheme only at the end of a word (pantai, pulau); elsewhere two vowel letters are two graphemes (main, laut, daun).

bashkir-ba.ambiguities: none in the standard orthography: ғ /ʁ/, ҡ /q/, ҙ /ð/, ҫ /θ/, ң /ŋ/, һ /h/ are single letters, so гъ, къ, нг are not Bashkir digraphs. The corpus nevertheless contains гъ (0.4% of types: мәгълүмат, игътибар, ягъни) and къ (0.2%: тәкъдим, икътисад) – these are Tatar spellings (Bashkir standard: мәғлүмәт, иғтибар, йәғни, тәҡдим), i.e. Tatar admixture in the corpus; a the tool's authors could add гъ /ʁ/ and къ /q/ as in the Tatar entry if that admixture is to be tolerated. ый (2.9%: ҡыйммәт, батырҙый) = ы+й; vowel+у/ү (ау, әү, ыу, еү = /aw/ /æw/ /ɯw/ /ew/) = vowel + glide, two graphemes.
bashkir-ba.notes: 42-letter alphabet; ъ is a Russian-loan separator (объект) or hamza mark. Doubled consonants (аттар, loan класс) are one long phoneme. Letter 'в' = /v~w/ in loans; native /w/ after vowels is written у/ү.

basque-eu.ambiguities: ts/tz/tx = t + s/z/x only across compound boundaries (bat + zuk → batzuk is in fact the affricate; genuine t+s sequences are essentially absent in standard spelling); ll/dd/tt = two single letters only in rare loans (e.g. 'ballet'); rr always a digraph. Automatic palatalisation after i (il, in → /ʎ/ /ɲ/ in some dialects: 'mutil', 'baina') is NOT written in Batua and is not a grapheme. Vowel sequences ai, ei, oi, ui, au, eu are diphthongs usually analysed as two phonemes – not listed.

multigraphs.note: trill, contrasts with single r /ɾ/ between vowels (erre vs ere)

basque-eu.notes: Standard Basque (Euskara Batua) is nearly fully transparent; x = /ʃ/, z = /s̻/, s = /s̺/, j = /j/ or /x/ (dialect/loan-dependent), h silent in Spain, ñ /ɲ/ single letter. c, q, v, w, y occur in loans/names only. Doubled vowels do not occur natively (zoo-type loans aside).

belarusian-be.ambiguities: д+з / д+ж across the boundary of the prefixes ад-, пад-, над-, перад- (падземны, адзначыць, падзел vs genuine падзея); doubled дд before з (аддзел, аддзяленне, ~0.1% of types) must be parsed д+дз, not дд+з – the doubles rule gets this wrong if applied first. ў is a separate letter /w/.

multigraphs.note: palatalised before е ё і ю я ь (дзе, дзень, будзе, людзі – this is the normal dzekanne reflex of soft д); дзь (будзь, ледзь) = +ь rule on the digraph

belarusian-be.notes: ь = palatalisation (соль, пісьмо, дзьве); apostrophe separator removed by the pipeline. Long (doubled) consonants – ззянне, жыццё, калоссе, насенне – are one long phoneme. Academic (1959/2008) orthography is dominant; Taraškievica texts would show more ь (зьява, сьвет) but the digraphs are the same.

bengali-bn.notes: Abugida: each consonant letter and each vowel sign (or the inherent vowel) is one grapheme, so the graphemic level equals the orthographic (akshara-based) one.

bikol-bcl.ambiguities: Doubled vowels = two syllables with glottal stop (maaram, nagkaaraki). ty/ts/sy/dy/ny/ly are listed by Wikipedia as the spellings of borrowed phonemes /tʃ ʃ dʒ ɲ ʎ/, but in native words the same letter pairs are C+/j/ across syllables, and in English loans in the corpus (city, variety, deputy) ty is t+y. The corpus also contains unassimilated Spanish/English spellings (ciudad, guerra, torre, branch).

multigraphs.note: single letter of the 2012 Giya sa Ortograpiyang Bikol alphabet (abakada + ng); word-initial in ngonyan, ngunyan

bikol-bcl.notes: Central (Naga/Legazpi) Bikol: 16 native consonants, 3 native vowels (a i u) plus marginal /e/; diphthongs /ai au iu ui/ are written with y/w (vowel + glide) and not listed. The pipeline alphabet keeps the stress/glottal diacritics á ó í â and ñ as single letters; they form no multigraphs. ñ appears only in 2 corpus types (año, años) and is normally respelled ny. Decision: the loan spellings ts, sy, dy, ny, ty, ly are treated as consonant + y/s sequences, not graphemes; only ng is merged.

sources.title: Comparison of orthographies of languages of the Philippines – Wikipedia

bishnupriya-bpy.notes: Abugida: each consonant letter and each vowel sign (or the inherent vowel) is one grapheme, so the graphemic level equals the orthographic (akshara-based) one.

bosnian-bs.ambiguities: Same as Croatian: nj = n+j in Latin loans (injekcija, konjunkcija), dž = d+ž after nad-/od- (nadživjeti), both rare. Doubled letters only at morpheme boundaries.
bosnian-bs.notes: Bosnian uses Gaj's Latin alphabet identically to Croatian (also officially Cyrillic, but the alphabet column shows Latin only); ije/je yat reflexes as in Croatian; h is retained in more words than in Serbian (kahva, lahko). No other digraphs.

breton-br.ambiguities: ou + vowel = /w/ + V (douar is dou-ar: /u/ + /a/ or /w/ – realisations vary); oa, oe, ui are glide + vowel (/wa/, /wɛ/, /ɥi/ – two phonemes, not listed, so longest-match correctly leaves them as two letters, but ou-a/ou-e sequences get ou merged which is right). gw/kw are /ɡw/ /kw/ (two phonemes). zh is always one unit in Peurunvan; z+h does not occur. c'hw = /xw/ or /f/ (two phonemes or one, dialectal). ñ only ever follows a vowel. nn, ll, rr, mm, tt mark a short preceding vowel and are one phoneme; ss is the only double with its own value. Diphthongs ae/ao/aou/ei: Wikipedia lists them as units but Breton phonological descriptions vary (some treat them as V + glide); users may demote them.

breton-br.notes: The corpus is in Peurunvan (ZH, 1941), the orthography used on Breton Wikipedia and in schools; texts in Skolveurieg (marked by é, final voiced letters) or the Interdialectal system may occur in minority. Vowel length is phonemic and partly marked by circumflex (â ê î ô û); final obstruents devoice (bag /bak/) but are spelled voiced; v after ñ is silent (añv = /ã/). The apostrophe in c'h is the only use of ' in the alphabet column.

bulgarian-bg.ambiguities: дз after the prefixes над-, под-, пред- (надзор, подземен, предзнаменование) is д+з – these are more common than true дз, so a users might prefer to drop дз; дж across a prefix boundary (надживея) is rare. йо (йод, майор) = /j/+/o/, two graphemes.

bulgarian-bg.notes: ъ is a full vowel letter /ɤ/ (българин, път), never a hardness mark. Iotated ю я = /j/+V or palatalisation+V, single letters; щ = /ʃt/ one letter. Doubled consonants (пролетта, странна, военна) arise at morpheme boundaries and are pronounced as one long consonant.

buryat-bxr.ambiguities: Doubled vowels (аа, ээ, ии, оо, өө, уу, үү) are the regular spelling of long vowels. Vowel + й across a morpheme boundary before a vowel is rare. ъ is only a divider before iotated vowels and is not a grapheme. н spells both /n/ and /ŋ/ (no digraph).

buryat-bxr.notes: Literary Buryat (Khori-based) in the 1939 Cyrillic alphabet: Russian letters plus ү ө һ (/h/). Orthography is close to Mongolian: long vowels by doubling, palatalisation by ь or by и/е/ё/ю/я after the consonant. Russian loanwords keep Russian spelling (ф, ц, ч, щ, ь).

catalan-ca.ambiguities: ts: the plural ending -ts after t-final stems (gats, tots, fets) is enormously more frequent than true /ts/ (potser, tsar); longest match would read 3500 corpus types with t+s as one grapheme — recommend NOT applying ts word-finally, or dropping it (only ~30 genuine cases). ig: the digraph only word-finally after a vowel (vaig, puig); word-internally ig + vowel is i + g (aigua, sigui, igual: 1389 corpus hits, most of them NOT the digraph) — restrict to word-final position. ix after a consonant or word-initially does not occur in native words except with /ks/ (fixar = f+i+x). tg/tj/qu/gu/sc need their vowel-context restrictions (tg before a/o or a consonant is t+g); assimilated t+C clusters (setmana /mm/, cotna /nn/, Betlem /ll/, ritme) are left as two graphemes. tll (bitllet, ratlla) tokenises as t + ll which matches its /ʎː/ value. ch in the corpus (174 types) is almost all English/foreign names plus archaic surnames (-ch = /k/); not listed. Diphthongs (ai, ei, oi, ui, au, eu, iu, ou, ia, ie, io, ua, ue, uo) are vowel + glide and not listed; ï/ü mark hiatus (raïm, taüt).

catalan-ca.notes: IEC standard; the interpunct · is in the alphabet so l·l is listed. Doubled consonants mm, nn, bb, dd, gg, pp, tt, cc are geminates (one long phoneme; innocent, setmana) — doubles 'one'; doubled vowels (reeixir, zoo) are two syllables but rare. Geminate/assimilation clusters tl, tll, tm, tn, ntm, ntn and foreign ch/sh/th/kh/ph are mentioned by Wikipedia; only native digraphs are listed above. Context rules applied: ts not at the end of a word (the plural -ts is t + s), ig only at the end of a word (vaig), tg only before e/i and tj before a/o/u, qu/gu only before e/i, sc only before e/i.

cebuano-ceb.ambiguities: Same as Tagalog: ts/ty/sy/dy/ny are often C+/j/ clusters; English loans in the corpus (city, authority, projects, body) will be mis-tokenised by longest match. Doubled vowels = two syllables with a glottal stop (maayo, gikaayo), never one long vowel.

cebuano-ceb.notes: Cebuano has a 3-vowel native system (a i u; e and o from Spanish); no vowel digraphs. The lexicon contains many unassimilated English/Spanish spellings (chairman, cash, illegal, requirements, council, poblacion) that follow English/Spanish, not Cebuano, grapheme rules; they were not listed. Older Spanish-era Cebuano spelling (c, qu, gui) is absent from the corpus except in proper names. Decision: the loan spellings ts, sy, dy, ny, ty, ly are treated as consonant + y/s sequences, not graphemes; only ng is merged.

chechen-ce.ambiguities: ъ is a letter for the glottal stop only word-finally or when doubled; elsewhere it is a syllable divider (шелъелла) and stands alone. ь appears only inside the graphemes listed here (хь, аь, оь, уь, яь, юь, ёь) and as a divider where ъ would be misread (кьх ≠ къ + х); Chechen has no C+ь palatalisation rule. ӏ alone = /ʕ/ (single letter) – after г к п т ц ч х it is always part of a digraph. Risky sequences for longest match: кх vs к+х (rare, across morphemes), хк (a cluster /xk/ that Komen lists as a grapheme – not included), дз/дж in loanwords (д+з rare), ай/ой/уй/ей/ов/ев/эв where й or в begins the next morpheme (e.g. -ов- in loans, йа- sequences) – moderately frequent, so users may prefer to keep only the ь-vowels, ий and уьй as vowel multigraphs.

chechen-ce.notes: Standard literary Chechen (Cyrillic, 1938 alphabet). The palochka was lowercased to ӏ in the data; it is a single letter for /ʕ/ and the second element of the ejective/fricative digraphs. Vowel length is mostly unwritten (а = /a/ and /aː/), so pseudowords cannot control length except via ий/уьй. Doubled consonants (пп, тт, сс, ккх) are geminates = one long consonant. The diphthong set (ай ой уй ей ов ев эв, уо ие) is listed following Komen (2007) and Nichols (1997); treatment of й/в-final diphthongs as single phonemes is a modelling decision. Decision: vowel + й / в diphthong spellings are not merged (they often span morpheme boundaries); only the ь-vowels, ий, уьй, уо and ие count as single vowel graphemes.

sources.title: Komen, E. R. (2007, unpublished manuscript). A proposal for a Chechen orthography (Radboud University)

chuvash-cv.ambiguities: none: ӑ ӗ ҫ ӳ are single letters; дж, нг occur only in loans/names (two graphemes). Palatalisation is otherwise carried by the following front vowel letter (е, ӗ, и, ӳ) and is not written. ъ is a Russian-loan separator (0.2% of types).
chuvash-cv.notes: Voicing of consonants between vowels/after sonorants is allophonic and NOT written (only voiceless letters in native words; б г д ж з ф ц щ appear in Russian loans). Geminates written by doubling (виҫҫӗ, тӑххӑр, пӗрре) are one long (fortis) consonant → doubles = one. Iotated е ё ю я are single letters.

In the southern variety dd = /ɖɖ/ (quiddu, eddu, cavaddu: 109 types) but it is covered by the general doubled-letter rule; ddh (4 types) is a rare variant.

Context rules applied as in Italian: ci/gi (and sci, sgi) count as one grapheme only before a/o/u, gli before a vowel, ch/gh/sc/sg only before e/i.

danish-da.ambiguities: Danish is a deep orthography: the vowel letters have many values and d/g/v after vowels are usually glides or silent (soft d [ð], g in -ig /i/, -nd/-ld with silent d) – these are single letters with context-dependent values rather than multigraphs, so transparency will be overestimated. hv/hj only word-initially (or compound-initially); h+v across compounds rare. ej/aj/øj: the j is a semivowel consonant phonologically, so users may prefer not to merge them; they are listed because standard GPC descriptions treat them as diphthong spellings. ng across boundaries (ingen fine; an-gå rare). ds (plads) /s/ and other silent-letter combinations are not listed.

dhivehi-dv.notes: Thaana is an alphabet with obligatory vowel diacritics (fili): every consonant letter carries exactly one fili (ަ ާ ި ީ ު ޫ ެ ޭ ޮ ޯ, long vowels are separate signs) or the sukun ް ('no vowel'); each letter and each fili is one grapheme, so there are no multigraphs. Three conventions a researcher should know: (1) alifu އ is a silent carrier for vowel-initial syllables (އަ އި … = the bare vowel; 30,489 corpus types), analogous to Uyghur ئ – not listed because the tool treats fili as separate vowel letters anyway; (2) alifu + sukun (އް, 12,680 types) geminates the following consonant (ބައްޕަ, މައްސަލަ) and word-finally spells a glottal stop; (3) noonu without any fili before a stop (ރަނގަޅު, ލަނޑު) marks prenasalisation, and noonu + sukun (ން) is /n/ or geminates a following nasal. Consonant letters are never doubled (gemination is written via އް), so doubles = n/a; doubled fili in the corpus (ަަ 100 types) are typos.

dutch-nl.ambiguities: sch is s+ch (/sx/) except word-finally and in -isch(e) where it is /s/: the tool should not treat sch as one unit, but will then read -isch as i+s+ch with a spurious /x/. ch after s in loans is /ʃ/ (schwung) – rare. Vowel pairs across syllable boundaries are usually disambiguated by the diaeresis (zeeën, geïnd, reëel), so false digraphs are rare; exceptions: ie in -ieel/-ieën, eu in museum, oe in poëzie-type words are written with diaeresis. eeuw/ieuw before a vowel (leeuwen) still one unit. ng across prefix boundary (aangaan). -tje after s/n (kastje, hondje → dj/tj).

eastern_mari-mhr.notes: Meadow (Eastern) Mari literary language: Russian alphabet plus ӓ-less set ҥ ӧ ӱ. Orthography is largely phonemic; ы = /ə/. Affricates ц ч are single letters. erzya-myv.notes: Erzya Mordvin uses the unmodified Russian alphabet; affricates ц ч are single letters and there are no vowel digraphs (ы = /ɨ/, э = /e/). The only multigraph pattern is consonant + ь. Beware that the corpus may contain Moksha texts, which use the same alphabet but a different phonology (voiceless l/r, ә written as а/о).

If diphthong units are wanted diphthong units, add aŭ and eŭ (V) – epitran lists aj aŭ ej eŭ oj uj. The corpus contains some h-system/x-system substitutes for the diacritic letters (ch, sh, gh, jh: ~160 types each for ch, sh, e.g. 'chu', 'shi') and English/loan names; these are not standard spellings. Doubled letters arise only across morpheme boundaries (mal-longa, dis-solvi) and are two phonemes.
esperanto-eo.notes: Strictly one letter – one phoneme (Fundamento 1905); the only optional digraph is dz for those who treat /d͡z/ as a phoneme (edzo). ĉ ĝ ĥ ĵ ŝ ŭ are single letters.

estonian-et.notes: One letter = one phoneme. Doubled letters spell long (quantity 2) or overlong (quantity 3) sounds; the orthography does not distinguish the two, so doubling is one grapheme. Palatalisation of d l n s t is not written. š and ž are single letters for loans (c, q, w, x, y, z, f appear only in foreign words/names). ng is n+g (allophonic [ŋ] before g/k).

french-fr.ambiguities: Two systematic issues. (1) NASAL VOWEL GRAPHEMES are context-dependent: V+n/V+m is one nasal grapheme only when followed by a consonant letter other than n/m, or at word end; before a vowel letter, or before a second n/m, the sequence is vowel + consonant (an-née, a-mi, i-nerte, o-nde vs. bon-ne, som-me). Plain longest-match would therefore wrongly nasalise ami, animal, fine, une, bonne, flamme, innocent, and would split moine/pointe/plaine/reine as oin/ain/ein + e instead of oi/ai/ei + n + e. The tokeniser needs the rule 'absorb n/m into the vowel grapheme only if the next letter is a consonant other than n/m, or there is no next letter'; with that rule the residual errors are lexical (enn- in ennui /ɑ̃n/, emm in femme /am/, word-final -ent of verbs, -um /ɔm/, European-type -éen) and rare in pseudowords. (2) SILENT LETTERS: French spells many silent final consonants (-s, -t, -d, -x, -z, -p, -ent) and a silent final -e; the grapheme count therefore overstates the phoneme count for most words, and the status of -er/-ez/-et (/e/, /ɛ/) is a the tool's authors decision (Manulex/Lexique-style GPC tables treat er, ez, et, est as vowel graphemes; this list does not, so word-final r/z/t are counted as consonant graphemes). Other longest-match errors: ge before e/i/consonant (germe, gel, genre — ge must be limited to a/o/u), gu before a/o (figure, aigu — limit to e/i/y), sc before a/o/u/consonant (escale), il after a consonant (fil, avril — limit il to vowel+il at word end), ill word-initially (illustre), ch /k/ in Greek words, gn in stagner, th/ph/ch across morpheme boundaries (almost never in native words), eu /y/ in forms of avoir, ill /il/ in ville/mille, ay/ey/oy before a consonant (Raymond, Reynaud: rare proper names), word-final um /ɔm/.

ganda-lg.notes: Standard 1947 orthography, very regular. Doubled consonants (bb, dd, gg, kk, ll, mm, nn, pp, ss, tt, zz, and nny, ggw) are geminates = one long phoneme; doubled vowels are long vowels = one phoneme (baana vs bana). l and r are one phoneme (r after e/i). h, q, x only in loanwords.

georgian-ka.notes: Mkhedruli is strictly phonemic: 33 letters, one letter = one phoneme, no digraphs (affricates ც ძ წ ჩ ჯ ჭ and fricatives შ ჟ ღ ხ are single letters). Doubled letters are two phonemes (გააკეთა = a+a across a prefix boundary; consonant doubles only across morpheme boundaries).

german-de.ambiguities: Dehnungs-h digraphs (ah, eh …) are wrong whenever h starts the next syllable (gehen, sehen, Reihe, Ruhe are fine as long vowel + silent h, but Ehe, Ahorn, behalten, Gehalt have a pronounced /h/); frequent, so users may prefer to drop the Vh digraphs. ch after s is sch, but -chen after s (Häuschen) is s+ch. ng across prefix boundaries (angeben). Nk is /ŋk/ (two phonemes) and chs is /ks/ (two phonemes): not listed. Vowel pairs across boundaries (beinhalten ei, Museum eu, Beamte ea).

gilaki-glk.notes: Gilaki has no official orthography; glk.wikipedia writes it in the Persian alphabet with Persian conventions (Ahmadi & Anastasopoulos 2023 report the script is almost identical to Persian's; Gilaki additionally uses a few extra letters/diacritics that the pipeline removed), so at the letter level it behaves like Persian: consonants letter-per-phoneme, ا و ی as vowel letters, short vowels mostly unwritten, ZWNJ as a word-internal separator (255 corpus types), no digraphs. Spelling is noticeably less consistent than Persian (competing conventions for /ə/, /o/ and the copula, e.g. ؤ/و, أ/ا, ئ/ی) – users may prefer status 'exclude' on those grounds; 'none' is given because the dominant system has no multigraphs whichever variant is used. The Persian remarks on خوا and initial ا+و/ی apply.

greek-el.notes: Monotonic Modern Greek. Doubled consonants (λλ, σσ, ττ, μμ, ρρ, κκ, ππ, νν) spell a single consonant; γγ is the exception (listed). Final ς is a positional variant of σ, not a separate phoneme. Whether αυ/ευ/ηυ count as graphemes is a the tool's authors decision (they map to two phonemes); the six entries marked EXCEPTION can be dropped with overrides.json.

Loanwords from Danish (bygderne, kommune, oktober, dansk) are frequent in the corpus and use Danish letters (b c d h w x y z æ ø å) and sequences.

Doubled vowels are phonologically long vowels (bimoraic) and are treated as one grapheme by the doubling rule.

guarani-gn.ambiguities: The letter g̃ /ŋ/ (tilded g) was stripped to g by the pipeline, so g can stand for /ɰ/ or /ŋ/ and n + g̃ (rare) would merge with ng. n + t across morpheme boundaries is more common than the marginal digraph nt — users may drop nt. Nasal vowels are single tilded letters, and the acute accent marks stress only. The apostrophe (puso) is the glottal-stop letter, not a modifier, so no apostrophe combinations.

guarani-gn.notes: Official achegety (Paraguay 1950/2018 standard) of 33 letters: digraphs ch, mb, nd, ng, nt, rr are counted as letters. Vowel sequences are separate syllables (no vowel multigraphs). Loanword letters b, c, d, f, l, q, x, z occur only in Spanish loans; older texts used y for /j/ and j for /dʒ/ differently.

gujarati-gu.notes: Abugida: each consonant letter and each vowel sign (or the inherent vowel) is one grapheme, so the graphemic level equals the orthographic (akshara-based) one.

The corpus contains untransliterated French (que, politique, février: qu, ph, th, ié) and English; these are not Creole graphemes.

haitian-ht.notes: Official 1979 IPN orthography (now overseen by the Akademi Kreyòl Ayisyen), fully phonemic; w, y are glide letters, r = /ɣ/. é is not an official letter (French residue). Doubled consonants do not occur natively except nn (one /n/ after an oral vowel). Context rule applied: an/en/on are nasal-vowel graphemes only when no vowel letter (or n/m) follows.

hausa-ha.ambiguities: kw/gw/ƙw/ky/gy/ƙy/fy are phonemic only before a/o/u (Hausa labialised/palatalised consonants); before i/e the sequences k+y etc. do not occur, so longest match is safe. The apostrophe ' is the glottal stop letter (word-internal: sa'a) and is also the first element of 'y; it is not written word-initially. ts: no competing t+s. sh: s+h across a boundary is rare (e.g. in compounds). Geminate digraphs are written by doubling the first letter (tsts? no: ssh, tts) — rare.

hausa-ha.notes: Boko (Latin) orthography; tone and vowel length are not marked in standard writing, so there are no doubled vowels (some textbooks write aa for long vowels, not in this corpus). Doubled consonants (babba, gidanka → gidanka, kakkarfa) are phonemic geminates = one long consonant, hence doubles = one. c = /tʃ/, j = /dʒ/ are single letters; hooked ɓ ɗ ƙ ƴ are single letters. r covers both /r/ and /ɽ/.

hebrew-he.ambiguities: Word-INITIAL יי (397 of 6,687 יי-types, ~6%) spells /ji/ (ייתכן, יישוב, יידע, יין): a consonantal yod plus the vowel yod, i.e. two phonemes – longest match gets these wrong. All other doubled letters are two phonemes (ממשלה, הה-, ללכת, תת-), never a digraph. ווו = וו + ו (ווושינגטון) parses correctly by longest match.

multigraphs.note: ktiv male: consonantal vav is doubled in the middle of a word (תקווה, צוות, שווה); single vav initially and finally. Word-initial וו in the corpus is almost all foreign names with /v~w/ (וושינגטון, וויליאם) or the prefix ו- before a vav (וורוד = /u-v/), so treating initial וו as one grapheme is right most of the time.

ktiv male: consonantal yod is doubled in the middle of a word (בניין, הייתה, חייב, עדיין); word-finally יי spells the diphthong /aj/ or /ej/ (עליי, חיי, היי). Not doubled next to a mater lectionis (פרויקט, ראיה).

hebrew-he.notes: Modern Hebrew, unpointed ktiv male (Academy of the Hebrew Language rules). The script is consonantal: ו spells /v/, /o/ or /u/, י spells /j/, /i/ or /e/, א/ה/ע are consonants or silent; most vowels are unwritten, so grapheme–phoneme alignment is only partial. ש /ʃ/ vs /s/ (שׂ) and the plosive/fricative pairs ב כ פ (dagesh) are not distinguished in unpointed text. Final forms ך ם ן ף ץ are positional allographs. The geresh digraphs ג׳ ז׳ צ׳ (/dʒ ʒ tʃ/) need ׳, which is not in the alphabet column, so they are ignored (they appear as plain ג ז צ in the data).

hindi-hi.notes: Abugida: each consonant letter and each vowel sign (or the inherent vowel) is one grapheme, so the graphemic level equals the orthographic (akshara-based) one.

hungarian-hu.ambiguities: Compound and derivational boundaries where two single letters meet: z+s (házsor, egészség is fine: sz+s), c+s (malacság), g+y, n+y, t+y and d+z (vadzab) are read as digraphs by longest match; in compounds the full digraph is kept (nagygyűlés = gy+gy, handled correctly). Suffix simplification (egy+gyel = eggyel) is a genuine long digraph. Such boundary cases are a small fraction of types and essentially absent from pseudowords. Long doubled digraphs written across a line break (ssz vs sz-sz) do not occur in the data.

hungarian-hu.notes: Fully standard orthography (Hungarian Academy rules). ch /x/ or /h/ and old family-name spellings (cz, th, gh, eö, y=/i/) occur only in loans and names (technika, Széchenyi) and are not listed; x = /ks/, w = /v/, q(u) = /kv/ in loans. dz and dzs are counted as graphemes/phonemes by the Academy although some phonologists treat dz as a cluster. Doubled single letters (tt, ll, ss) and doubled vowels do not occur as graphemes except the listed long digraphs; vowel length is marked by acute accent letters that are in the alphabet.

icelandic-is.ambiguities: hv is [kʰv] (two phonemes) and is not listed; hj/hl/hn/hr are only word-initial, elsewhere h+C across compound boundaries (e.g. 'hálfleikur'). ll/nn: value depends on the preceding vowel and on the word being native; longest match will tokenise all ll/nn as one grapheme, which is right as a grapheme but the phoneme (tl vs. lː) must be looked up by context. rl, rn, fl, fn, sl, sn have epenthetic/pre-stopped realisations ([rtl], [tn], [pl], [pn], [stl]) but are clusters of two graphemes. ng/nk are /ŋk/ or /ŋ/ + stop: not listed. Pre-aspirated pp/tt/kk ([hp ht hk]) are the ordinary doubling convention. ei/ey/au across boundaries are very rare because compounds are written together but the diphthongs are so frequent that the error rate is negligible.

icelandic-is.notes: Icelandic is otherwise very transparent; accented letters (á é í ó ú ý) are separate single letters. ll and nn are included because they have a value different from l+l/n+n in the dominant native-word case.

igbo-ig.ambiguities: n+w and n+y: the syllabic nasal prefix n- before w/y (n + we) would be merged into nw/ny by longest match; this is uncommon but real. gh vs g+h, kw vs k+w: no competing sequences. Doubled consonants are almost always syllabic nasal + nasal (mm, nn in mmadụ, nne) = two units; doubled vowels (ọọ, aa, ee in ndeewo) are two syllables, so doubles = two.
igbo-ig.notes: Ọnwụ (1961) standard alphabet of 36 letters: 8 vowels including dotted ị ọ ụ and the velar nasal ṅ (single letter); tone is not written in the corpus. The alphabet column contains c, q, x which occur only in loanwords; c occurs natively only in ch. Dialectal digraphs (gbh, ṅw, kpw) of the New Standard Orthography are not standard.

ilocano-ilo.ambiguities: Consonant gemination is phonemic and very frequent (lallaki, ubbing, keddeng, nagbabasa) — doubled consonants are one long consonant, but doubled VOWELS are two syllables separated by a glottal stop (saan /sa.ʔan/; 'reduplicate vowels are not slurred together'), so the single 'doubles' setting cannot be right for both; consonant gemination is the more frequent phenomenon, hence 'one'. ll is a geminate /lː/ in native words (lallaki, allon, billit) and /lj/~/ʎ/ only in Spanish-based spellings of loans (caballo); it is covered by the doubling rule, not listed. rr is rare (17 types) and in a few English loans it is a mere spelling (berry).

ilocano-ilo.notes: Two spelling systems coexist: the Spanish-based one (c, qu, ll, gui) preferred by older writers and the Tagalog-based phonemic one (2022 Tarabay iti Ortograpia ti Pagsasao nga Ilokano: abakada + ng, with ll listed as a borrowed letter). The corpus is overwhelmingly Tagalog-based (qu: 2 types, c mostly in Latin plant names), so that system is described. Diphthongs aw/ay/iw/oy/uy/ey are vowel + glide; other vowel sequences (uo, ai) are separate syllables with a glottal stop (buok, dait). sy/dy/ny are virtually absent from the corpus (0–1 types) and were not listed; the corpus contains English/Latin botanical names (nightshade, dicotyledon, chinensis). Decision: the loan spellings ts, sy, dy, ny, ty, ly are treated as consonant + y/s sequences, not graphemes; only ng is merged.

indonesian-id.ambiguities: DECISION: EYD/PUEBI and most phonological descriptions (Indonesian: 'four diphthongs ai au oi ei') treat them as single units, so they are listed; but they are diphthongs only in open syllables, and an alternative analysis (vowel + glide /aj aw oj/) exists. Longest match will be wrong for every ai/au/oi followed by a consonant within the word (main, lain, kain, baik, naik, air, laut, daun, kaum, taun, poin) — these are at least as frequent as the true diphthongs — and across morpheme boundaries (gulai 'sweeten' = gula+i vs gulai 'curry'; di-ikuti, ke-uangan). A position rule 'diphthong only word-finally or before a suffix' would fix most cases; otherwise users may prefer to drop ai/au/oi/ei. ng + h (penghargaan) is ng+h, correctly handled by left-to-right longest match. Doubled consonants arise only at morpheme boundaries (lainnya = lain+nya, tahunnya) and doubled vowels are two syllables (saat, maaf, taat, keempat, diinginkan); 'nn' in lainnya must be tokenised n+ny, not nn+ya.

indonesian-id.notes: EYD (1972) / PUEBI (2015) / EYD V (2022) spelling: 26 letters; f, v, z, q, x only in loans; digraphs ng ny kh sy are not separate letters of the alphabet. gh (/ɣ/) is a Malaysian digraph; Indonesian replaces it with g (gaib) though maghrib is common — not listed. No lexicon for indonesian-id was present in the workspace, so attestation could not be checked (the Javanese/Sundanese/Banjar/Minangkabau corpora, which contain much Indonesian, show ai 400–700 and au 130–430 types each). Epitran additionally lists nc/nj (as ɲc/ɲj), which are n + c/j, not digraphs. Decision: the diphthong spellings (ai, au, oi, ei) count as one grapheme only at the end of a word (pantai, pulau); elsewhere two vowel letters are two graphemes (main, laut, daun).

irish-ga.notes: RECOMMENDATION for Irish and Scottish Gaelic vowels: the pronounced unit is the whole vowel group between consonants, in which the letters flanking the consonants (e before a/o, i after a/o/u, a before í/ó/ú …) are silent markers of consonant quality under 'caol le caol agus leathan le leathan'. A reading researcher (cf. Stenson & Hickey 2018, Understanding Irish Spelling) would want (a) tokenisation of any maximal run of vowel letters as ONE vowel grapheme ('vowel-group' rule), with the fada-bearing or stressed letter as nucleus – this is equivalent to longest match over the list above except for hiatus words, and is the treatment we recommend; or (b) if the tool cannot do that, exclude Irish/Gaelic from vowel-level grapheme counts and report consonant graphemes only, because a letter-level vowel count is meaningless here. Consonant-quality marking means the same phoneme /a/ is spelled a, ea, ai, eai – orthographic depth is high in the V→P direction but the system is rule-governed. Acute letters (á é í ó ú) are long vowels; y, j, k, q, v, w, x, z occur in loans only. Context rule applied: the eclipsis spellings mb, gc, nd, bhf, bp, dt, ts count as one grapheme only at the start of a word. Runs of vowel letters are merged as far as the listed digraphs and trigraphs allow, following the recommendation that under caol le caol the glide letters mark consonant quality rather than vowels.

italian-it.ambiguities: ci/gi/sci/gli are digraphs only before a/o/u (ci before e, i or a consonant is c+i: cibo, cinema, cifra; gi likewise: giro, ginocchio; gli before i or a consonant: glicine (exception), and word-internal gl+consonant never occurs). ch/gh/sc are digraphs only before e/i (sch before e/i = s + ch /sk/: schema, maschio — two graphemes, correct under longest match once sch is NOT listed). cc+e/i = /ttʃ/, gg+e/i = /ddʒ/ and cci/ggi + a/o/u are geminate affricates: the doubles rule (cc = one grapheme) gives the right count for cce/cci but needs cci/ggi listed so that caccia is not cc + ia. qu = /kw/ (two phonemes, not listed); cqu as in acqua = cq + u. gn in a few learned words is /ɡn/ (gnostico, wagneriano), gl+i /ɡli/ in glicine, negligente, anglicano. Diphthongs (ia, ie, io, iu, ua, ue, uo, ui, ai, ei, oi, au, eu) are glide + vowel and not listed; z = /ts/ or /dz/ is a single letter.

italian-it.notes: Very transparent orthography. Doubled consonants are geminates (one long phoneme). The corpus alphabet includes both grave and acute accented vowels (è/é, ò/ó) and also ì/í, ù/ú (í/ú are non-standard typing variants). h alone is silent (ho, hai). Context rules applied: ci/gi/sci/cci/ggi only before a/o/u (ciao, giorno; in cibo the i is a vowel), gli before a vowel and gl before i (famiglia, figli), ch/gh/cch/ggh and sc only before e/i.

javanese-jv.ambiguities: th/dh in English loans (the, with) are t+h or English th; dh/th never arise across a native morpheme boundary. ngg = ng+g (kanggo, nanging) is handled by left-to-right longest match; ngh = ng+h (sanghyang). Vowel sequences ai, au (yaiku, saiki, main, laut, taun) are two syllables in Javanese and are not listed, although Indonesian loanwords in the corpus contain the Indonesian diphthongs (sampai, atau). Doubled consonants only at morpheme boundaries or in the possessive/suffix -ké (anakku, dhèwèké); doubled vowels are two syllables (maaf, kaanan, perusahaan).

javanese-jv.notes: Modern Latin Javanese (1972/2011 Pedoman) 'is generally the same as the Indonesian alphabet' with é /e/, è /ɛ/, e /ə/ and the retroflex digraphs dh, th. The corpus is inconsistent in writing the accents (dheweke vs dhèwèké, both present) and has Indonesian and English loans (chip, flash, show) plus a few pre-1972 forms (djadi, tjarita, oe). Vowel allophony (a → /ɔ/ in open final syllables, i/u → ɪ/ʊ in closed syllables) is not marked.

kannada-kn.notes: Abugida: each consonant letter and each vowel sign (or the inherent vowel) is one grapheme, so the graphemic level equals the orthographic (akshara-based) one.

kapampangan-pam.ambiguities: ai/au across a morpheme boundary (ma-igit, ka-ugnayan, Tagalog loans) are two syllables; given that the reduction to /ɛ/ /o/ is dialect-dependent and spelling varies (ai~e, au~o), users may prefer to drop these two vowel digraphs. ts/sy/ny/ly: cluster-vs-digraph caveat as for Tagalog. Doubled vowels are rare and represent two syllables.

multigraphs.note: single letter of the 2016 Bayung Ortograpiyang Kapampangan (Filipino-based) alphabet; /ŋ/ 'occurs in all positions, including the beginning of a word' (ngeni); extremely frequent in function words (ing, king, ning, reng)

kapampangan-pam.notes: Three competing Latin spellings exist: the Spanish-based súlat Bacolor (c, qu, gu, ll, ñ: queng, quing, queti), the indigenised súlat Guagua/abakada (k), and the Amung Samson hybrid; since 2016 the Filipino-based orthography is official. The corpus is dominated by the k-based system (qu: 21 types, mostly English; ng: 1272), so that is what is described; the ~10 Spanish-style tokens (queng, quing, queti, queang) are a secondary system in the data and would be mis-tokenised (qu = /k/). Standard Kapampangan has no /h/ in native words. Many unassimilated English/Spanish spellings (technology, cell, guerra, headquarters) are present and were not listed. Decision: the loan spellings ts, sy, dy, ny, ty, ly are treated as consonant + y/s sequences, not graphemes; only ng is merged. The ai/au spellings are not merged either.

kashubian-csb.notes: Kashubian alphabet (34 letters) per Wikipedia; the single letters ò (/wɛ/), ù (/wu/), ô (/ɞ/), ã, ą, é, ë carry the vowel system. The ni-before-vowel rule is inferred from Kashubian practice (Polish-style) rather than stated on the alphabet page; k/g before e/i are palatalised (/c ɟ/ or /t͡ɕ d͡ʑ/) without a written mark. Older texts in the corpus may use pre-1996 spellings. Context rule applied: ni is one grapheme only before a vowel letter.

kazakh-kk.ambiguities: none for native words: ғ қ ң ө ұ ү һ і ә are single letters. The letters и and у stand for vowel+glide sequences (/əj/ /ɪj/, /ʊw/ /ʉw/ /əw/) but are single letters, so the explicit sequences ый ій ұу үу ыу іу are vowel + й/у, two graphemes each – do not merge. дж /dʒ/ appears only in transliterated foreign names (Джон, джаз); нг is н+г across morpheme boundaries.
kazakh-kk.notes: ё ц ч щ ъ ь э are confined to Russian loanwords; ъ is a separator (объект, съезд); щ = long ш in three native words (ащы, тұщы, кеще). Doubled consonants (аттар = ат+тар, loan класс) are one long phoneme.

kinyarwanda-rw.ambiguities: Longest match gives shy > sh, cy > c, nshy = n+shy, ncy = n+cy, which is right. It is wrong for s+h and c+y across morpheme boundaries (rare). The glide sequences bw, pw, tw, rw, mw, nw, sw, zw, jw have unusual realisations ([bɡ], [pk], [tkw], [ɾɡw], [mŋ] ...) but are consonant + glide in spelling, so they are not listed. Vowel length is phonemic; the 2014 official orthography writes long vowels double (aa, ii, uu), but Wikipedia-era text often leaves them single, so doubled vowels are inconsistent in the corpus.

kinyarwanda-rw.notes: Standardised Latin orthography since the 1940s; Catholic and Protestant spelling differ slightly (e.g. use of y vs i). The prenasalised series is listed because Rwanda-Rundi phonology treats NC as single segments; users may drop it to treat N+C as two graphemes. p, pf are loan/rare. k and c alternate before i/e in some speakers (ki ~ ci).

komi-kv.ambiguities: і after д з л н с т marks the consonant as hard (ді = /di/, ди = /dʲi/) – single letter, no digraph. дз/дж/тш are unambiguous in native words; in Russian loans д+з, д+ж, т+ш clusters occur (подзем-, отшельник) but are rare. Doubled consonants (geminates such as сс, нн in вӧсна, ыджыд -> ыджыдджык) are pronounced long = one grapheme.

multigraphs.note: palatal voiced affricate; also дзь before consonant/finally

komi-kv.notes: Komi-Zyrian in the 1938 Cyrillic alphabet (Russian letters + ӧ, і). The three affricate digraphs are traditionally not counted as letters but are the standard spelling of distinct phonemes. ӧ = /ɘ/. ъ is only a divider in loanwords. Komi-Permyak shares exactly the same alphabet and digraphs.

komi_permyak-koi.ambiguities: Same as Komi-Zyrian: і after д з л н с т marks hardness (single letter); дз/дж/тш can be clusters in Russian loans (rare). Doubled consonants are geminates = one grapheme. Older (pre-1938) Komi-Permyak texts used extra letters; ignore.
komi_permyak-koi.notes: Komi-Permyak uses the same 35-letter Cyrillic alphabet (Russian + ӧ, і) and the same three affricate digraphs as Komi-Zyrian; orthographic principles are identical, differences are lexical/phonetic (e.g. Permyak л where Zyrian has в/l-alternation).

konkani-gom.ambiguities: ea (2155 types), eo, ie, ia spell palatalisation + vowel (amchea /amtʃja/, teo, ieta) — treated as e/i = /j/ + vowel, i.e. two graphemes, and not listed; ai oi au ou ui are vowel + glide (two phonemes). A word-final or pre-consonantal m/n after a vowel marks vowel nasalisation (hem, mhonnlem, bhurgeank: Ṽ) rather than a consonant; the tool will count it as a consonant. nv (-anv) is a nasalised vowel + v. x = /ʃ/ is a single letter. th/ph/sh/ch in English loans (the, photography, show, championship — 245 English words were removed but some remain) are not Konkani graphemes; sh in Konkani is x. Retroflex vs plain stops are only distinguished by doubling, so a long dental does not exist orthographically.

konkani-gom.notes: Romi (Roman-script Goan) Konkani following the Thomas Stephens Konknni Kendr / Dalgado Konkani Academy conventions, as in the Leipzig gom newscrawl corpus. Spelling is semi-standardised (TSKK 'Romi Lipient Konknni Borounchi Promann Rit'); ch for both /tʃ/ and /ts/, variable use of ts, and loanword spellings make it less regular than Devanagari Konkani. The nasal vowel letters ã ẽ ĩ õ of the formal standard were mostly stripped by the pipeline (only õ survives, 1 type).

kurdish-ku.ambiguities: وو is listed as a digraph, so the doubles rule must not treat it as و+و; genuine و+و (/w/+/u/, e.g. وون?) is negligible. یی (3,725 types, نییە /nijə/, -یی abstract suffix) is ی + ی = /ij/, two phonemes, consistent with doubles='two'. Word-internal ئ before a vowel in compounds (ڕۆژئاوا, بۆئەوەی, 400 types) is a syllable onset marker exactly as word-initially, so the ئ+V reading is still right; in Arabic loans (ئیسرائیل, قورئان) it is /ʔ/ – rare. Treat the ئ+V entries as 'vowel with silent carrier'; if the tool models ئ as a consonant /ʔ/ instead, drop them (the Wikipedia table gives ئ = [ʔ]). The epitran units نگ (=[ŋ], phonemically /n/+/g/: دەنگ) and یە (/j/+/ə/) are two phonemes each and deliberately not listed.

kurdish-ku.notes: Central Kurdish (Sorani) in Arabic script as on ckb.wikipedia (code kurdish-ku here). Letter-per-phoneme otherwise: ڕ ڵ ڤ ێ ۆ ە are single letters; ه (U+0647, 2,932 types) is /h/ and ە /a~ɛ/; و and ی are both vowel and glide, disambiguated only by context. ZWNJ (listed as a modifier) separates morphemes (له‌) and forms no grapheme. Some texts use Persian-style ه for final ە; the corpus is mostly consistent. نگ (/ŋ/) added after the epitran cross-check.

kyrgyz-ky.ambiguities: none: ң ө ү are single letters; нг (1.8% of types) is always н+г (e.g. dative/locative suffixes after н); дж only in foreign names. ъ is a separator in Russian loans (объект).
kyrgyz-ky.notes: Long vowels are written by doubling the vowel letter: аа оо уу өө үү ээ (and marginally ии, ее in loans; ыы does not occur) – each doubled vowel is ONE long phoneme, so the doubles rule applies with value 'one'. Vowel+й/у sequences (ай, ой, оу, ею) are two graphemes.

ladino-lad.ambiguities: ny before a vowel is the digraph (anyo, espanyola, sinyifika); n + y across a boundary practically never occurs, and word-initial/final ny does not occur. dj vs d+j: no counter-cases. In AY, gu is NOT a digraph: g is always /ɡ/ (gerra, gitara, sige) and gu before e/i is /ɡw/ (guevos, guesos, verguensa, linguistika) — do not import the Spanish gu/qu rules; qu occurs only in unadapted Spanish words (que, quien: 8 types). ll (11 types: valle, ellos, estrella) is Spanish/Italian spelling leakage and tz/kh/tch/ts (a handful of Hebrew/Nahuatl/English items) are not listed. y is a consonant /j/ between vowels (eya, famiya, yamar) and marks glides in ya/ye/yo (tyerra, tyempo); ia/ie/io/ua/ue/ai/ei/oi diphthongs are vowel + glide and not listed. The corpus is about 90% Aki Yerushalayim (k 2150 types vs c 167 mostly in ch, q 9), with a Spanish-spelled minority (que, quien, cuando) that the tokeniser will mishandle in a small number of items.

ladino-lad.notes: Latin-script Judaeo-Spanish in the Aki Yerushalayim (Shaul/Autoridad Nasionala del Ladino) orthography: phonemic, k for /k/, s for /s/, z for /z/, j for /ʒ/, dj for /dʒ/, ch, sh, ny, h for /h/ (haham, hue), no c/q/ñ/ll/accents (acute accents in the alphabet come from the Spanish-spelled minority). Competing Latin systems (Turkish-based with ş/ç, Spanish-based Ladinokomunita, French-based) and Hebrew/Rashi script are not represented in the corpus. Doubled letters other than rr are two sounds or loan spellings (kibbutz, polandball).

latin-la.ambiguities: eu is NOT listed: in this corpus it is mostly e+u across a morpheme boundary (deus, meus, eum, exeunte) and a true diphthong only in heu, seu, neu, Europa and Greek names; ui likewise (cui, huic diphthong vs fuit, quia = q+u+i). ae/oe are two vowels in a handful of words (aer, poeta, coegi). gu after n (lingua, sanguis) is a labiovelar /ɡʷ/ for some scholars but gu elsewhere (augustus, regula) is g+u, so it is not listed. gn = [ŋn] and ng = n+g are not graphemes. x = /ks/ (single letter, two phonemes). latvian-lv.ambiguities: dz = d+z and dž = d+ž essentially never (no d-final prefixes; pie-dzīvot etc. contain the affricate). ie = i+e in a few loans and across boundaries (pie-ēst). Vowel+j/v sequences (tavs, maijs) are pronounced as diphthongs but spelled with consonants, so they do not affect tokenisation. Doubled letters do not occur in native spelling (length uses macrons); lengthened intervocalic obstruents (lapa [lapːa]) are not written.

diphthong; Latvian phonology lists ai au ei ui iu oi as phonemic diphthongs, but a conservative count may treat them as V+V

ligurian-lij.ambiguities: sc before h (tedeschi, bòschi: 29 types vs 451 sc+e/i) = s+k; ci/gi/sci/scci are digraphs only before a, o, u (ci + vowel i or consonant: 329 types, e.g. ciü, circa); gl is only in Italianisms (famiglia, ingleize: 15 types, g+l in -ngl-). ei (zeneize, trei, 211 types) and ao (read as /au/, /ɔw/ or long o) are not listed: vowel + glide, two phonemes. eu in Italianisms (europea) is e+u. ñ (/ŋ/) and æ, ç, x are single letters.

ligurian-lij.notes: Dominant system is the grafia ofiçiâ of the Academia Ligustica do Brenno (æ, ç, x, ñ, circumflexes for length), which the corpus overwhelmingly follows (æ in 388 types, ç 691, x 317); a minority of pages use older or 'unitaria'-type spellings (ü/ö for /y/ /ø/, ~250 types), so vowel-level counts are slightly noisy. Doubled consonants mark a preceding short vowel (one grapheme); zz = /z/, çç = /s/. Intervocalic s is voiceless in this spelling, so ss is mere doubling. j is rare (gjêmo). Context rules applied as in Italian: ci/gi (and sci, sgi) count as one grapheme only before a/o/u, gli before a vowel, ch/gh/sc/sg only before e/i.

lithuanian-lt.ambiguities: ie/uo/ai/ei across prefix boundaries (pa-ieškoti, ne-išeiti, nu-eiti, pa-uostyti) – fairly frequent in real text but irrelevant for pseudowords; ch is unambiguous. The palatalisation marker i before back vowels (ia, ią, io, iu, iū, ių, iuo: čia, giaus, kiaušinis) is silent – the tool would count 'iuo' as i + uo and 'ia' as two vowels unless a rule 'C + i + back vowel → i belongs to the consonant' is added; this affects a large share of Lithuanian words. Doubling occurs only at prefix boundaries (perrašyti) and is two phonemes.

multigraphs.note: loanwords only (chemija, choras) but standard; treated as a two-letter sequence for collation

lithuanian-lt.notes: Consonants are automatically palatalised before e, ę, ė, i, į, y; before a, ą, o, u, ų, ū palatalisation is written with an inserted i. maltese-mt.notes: Maltese alphabet (1924/1992 Akkademja tal-Malti) is transparent apart from the silent letters h (silent except word-finally = /ħ/) and għ, whose effect on neighbouring vowels is rule-governed but complex; ċ ġ ħ ż are single letters; x = /ʃ/, q = /ʔ/, j = /j/, z = /t͡s/. y occurs only in loans and is in the vowel column of alphabets.tsv for that reason. manx-gv.ambiguities: ch is the main problem: /x/ (lenition of c/k) vs /tʃ/ (where Irish has slender c) is lexically determined and çh is used inconsistently; a tool should treat ch as one grapheme with two values. Consonant doubling (bb, dd, gg, ll, nn, rr, ss, tt, cc) marks a short preceding vowel and sometimes voicing (cc medially = /ɡ/, bb = /b/~/v/); one phoneme. Vowel spellings follow 17th-century English/Welsh conventions and are not rule-governed: the same sound is spelled several ways and the same spelling has several values (ey = /eː ɛː əː ə/); vowel + y/w sequences (ayr, bayr, keyl) and i/u glides also combine freely, so longest match will produce many arbitrary segmentations. Omniglot and Help:IPA/Manx do not give an exhaustive list.

maori-mi.ambiguities: ng and wh are unambiguous (n+g and w+h never occur otherwise). maori-mi.notes: Māori phonology: 10 consonants (p t k m n ng wh h r w), 5 vowels short/long; long vowels are single macron letters in the pipeline alphabet. mazanderani-mzn.notes: Mazanderani has no official orthography; mzn.wikipedia writes it in the Persian alphabet with Persian conventions (Ahmadi & Anastasopoulos 2023 report the script is almost identical to Persian's plus one added diacritic, removed by the pipeline), so at the letter level it behaves like Persian: consonants letter-per-phoneme, ا و ی as vowel letters, short vowels mostly unwritten, ZWNJ as a word-internal separator (1,385 corpus types), no digraphs. Spelling is noticeably less consistent than Persian (competing conventions for /ə/, /o/ and the copula, e.g. ؤ/و, أ/ا, ئ/ی) – users may prefer status 'exclude' on those grounds; 'none' is given because the dominant system has no multigraphs whichever variant is used. The Persian remarks on خوا and initial ا+و/ی apply.

mizo-lus.ambiguities: Mizo syllables/morphemes are written together in words and compounds, so boundary clashes occur: h-final morpheme + ch/hm/hn (tihchhuah = tih+chhuah, hmachhawn) is tokenised correctly (h, then chh); n-final + gh or ng-final + h-initial morpheme would be read as ngh, which is rare (lirnghing = lir+nghing and innghat = in+nghat are genuine ngh). Vowel + h at syllable end (tawh, pawh, chhuah, theih: h = final glottal /ʔ/~/h/) is a coda consonant, not part of a digraph, and 'wh' (229 types) is aw + h; the tokeniser must match aw before h, which longest-match does. aa, ii (hmaa, niin, thlaa) are vowel + vowel across suffix boundaries (two syllables) — the doubling rule should not merge them; set doubles n/a and let the tool treat them as two. Diphthongs ai au ei eu ia iu ua ui (and iai iau uai uau) are vowel + glide or glide + vowel in Mizo phonology and are not listed. The corpus (7,339 types) contains many English words (association, climate, championship, football).

mizo-lus.notes: Standard Mizo (Lushai) Roman alphabet (Lorrain 1894 tradition): 25 letters including the digraphs aw, ch, ng and the letter ṭ. Tone diacritics (circumflex = long, acute/grave = tone) are only partly kept in the data (â, á only). Voiceless sonorants are written h + sonorant; aspirated stops/affricates C + h; the lateral affricates tl / thl. Doubled vowels (aa, ii) are suffix sequences of two vowels, so they count as two graphemes.

Vowel + й before another vowel (e.g. -ийн, -ай-) is still diphthong + nothing, but й before a vowel at a morpheme boundary (хоёр vs хоюу) is rare. яй/ёй/юй are /j/ + diphthong and are not listed. ъ occurs only as a divider before я/ё/ю after a consonant (rare) and is not a grapheme. н before г is [ŋ] but нг is a cluster, not a digraph.

mongolian-mn.notes: Khalkha Mongolian in Cyrillic. Long vowels are spelled by doubling; palatalisation is marked by ь (морь), by и, or by the iotated vowels е ё ю я after the consonant (do not merge consonant + iotated vowel). Non-initial single vowel letters are usually reduced/epenthetic. Whether ай/ой/уй/үй/эй count as one phoneme or vowel + /j/ is a modelling choice; most phonologies of Khalkha list them as diphthong phonemes.

navajo-nv.ambiguities: Longest match is right for tłʼ > tł, tsʼ > ts, chʼ > ch, dz, dl, gh, hw. The letter x is written after s/sh/ts/ch to show that a following h is a separate fricative (e.g. tsxį́į́łgo), so x+h-type sequences are not digraphs. ʼ (U+02BC) alone is the glottal stop letter, also used word-initially before vowels in some spellings (ʼaʼáán). Tone marks were stripped, so aá/áa rising-falling contours collapse to aa. The diphthongs ai, ei, oi are marginal and mostly tonal contours over two vowels; users may drop them.

navajo-nv.notes: Young & Morgan (1980s) standard orthography: 4 vowels a e i o with length by doubling and nasality by ogonek (nasal hooks kept); long vowels are single phonemes (doubles = one). b d g j are voiceless unaspirated, ł is a single letter. Stem-initial consonant clusters across prefix boundaries (e.g. d + l in -d-ló-? ) can create spurious dl/dz/ts readings but these are regular phonological units anyway.

northern_frisian-frr.ambiguities: Corpus mixes dialect orthographies: Fering-Öömrang (faan, det, uun, diar, wiar – the largest share), Mooring (dåt, önj, foon, än, jü; letters å) and Sölring (đ, ā, ē: üđer, eeđer, kām), plus a few Halunder/Goesharde forms. The multigraph conventions (double long vowels, ch/sch/ng/nj/lj/tj/dj, ia/ua diphthongs) are shared by the Fering-Öömrang and Mooring systems, so the list above is valid for roughly 90% of word types; the Sölring ā/ē letters are single letters and đ is a single letter. ia/ua are one diphthong phoneme in Fering/Mooring but i+a across boundaries occurs (regiuun, prowins loans). tj/dj/nj/lj across syllable boundaries are rare.

northern_frisian-frr.notes: Northern Frisian has no unified orthography; each island/mainland dialect has its own (Nordfriisk Instituut conventions from the 1970s share the main rules). öi, uai and oi exist in Fering but are unattested in this corpus and were dropped. Lexicon is tiny (3.7k types) and dialect-mixed, so grapheme statistics will be noisy; users may prefer to exclude or restrict to Fering/Mooring forms. German-influenced spellings (sch, ü, ö, ä) are standard in all systems.

northern_sami-se.ambiguities: The lexicon (6,286 types, Wikipedia + a small subtitle list) contains a visible share of Southern Sami words (daesnie, maehtieh, tjaebpie, lohkedh, ~1-2% of types) whose ie/oe/ae/tj/sj spellings do not follow the Northern Sami rules; users may want to filter words with ae, oe, ïe, tj, sj or final -dh. Within Northern Sami: dj/nj/lj across a syllable boundary are always the palatal consonant, but lj is occasionally /lːj/. Closing diphthongs (ái, ai, oi, ui, ij) are vowel + /j/ and are not listed. Preaspirated stops hp ht hk hc hč (and hpp htt …) and pre-stopped nasals dn tn bm pm gŋ kŋ (dnj tnj) are analysed as clusters (h+C, stop+nasal) in the Wikipedia/standard description and are not listed, although some phonologists treat them as unit phonemes; longest match therefore reads them as two graphemes, which matches the cluster analysis. Consonant-centre length is partly unwritten (Q2 vs Q3), so doubled letters may be long or overlong.

northern_sotho-nso.ambiguities: Longest match handles tšh > tš, tlh > tl, tsh > ts, pšh > pš, psh > ps. It is wrong where a syllabic nasal precedes an aspirated consonant: mph, nth, nkh, ntšh, ntlh, nts are N + Ch and the N is syllabic (nthuše = n̩.thu.še), which longest match still parses correctly as n + th. The real failures: hl vs tlh confusion is an orthographic problem among writers themselves (both occur for /ɬ/ ~ /tɬʰ/), and ng vs n+g across the class-9 prefix (n- + g...) is rare. Doubled nn (nna) is syllabic n + n (two units); doubled vowels are rare and two syllables.

norwegian-no.ambiguities: k/g/sk before i, y (and j) are /ç/ /j/ /ʂ/ without a digraph (kino, gi, ski) – single letters with context-dependent values; the tool cannot capture this. rt, rd, rn, rl are retroflex single segments [ʈ ɖ ɳ ɭ] in East Norwegian like rs but are usually analysed as /r/+C; only rs is listed (a matter of choice – drop rs for consistency if preferred). rs across morpheme boundaries (for-søk → /ʂ/ anyway in East Norwegian). sl within a morpheme is /ʂl/. eg/øg in meg, deg, seg, regn, løgn are pronounced /æi/ /œy/ but spelled with g: not listed. -ig/-lig has silent g; -nd/-ld has silent d: single letters. ei across compound boundaries (kafé-eier) rare. gn is /ŋn/ (two phonemes), not listed.
norwegian-no.notes: Corpus is Bokmål (no.wikipedia). Norwegian vowel letters are single graphemes (é only in a few loans). sj/skj/kj are the only frequent consonant multigraphs; sch/ch occur only in names and loans and are omitted. Decision: the retroflex spellings rs/rt/rd/rn/rl are not merged (none of them is a grapheme in standard descriptions, and merging only rs would be inconsistent).

norwegian_nynorsk-nn.ambiguities: Same as Bokmål: k/g/sk before i/y are palatal without a digraph; rt/rd/rn/rl retroflex not listed; eg/øg (meg, seg, regn) diphthongal but spelled with g; silent d in -nd/-ld; silent g in -ig/-leg. ei across boundaries rare.

occitan-oc.notes: The corpus is overwhelmingly in the classical (Alibertine) norm (ò 1544 types, lh 597, nh 421 vs. Mistralian 'ou' ~130), with a sizeable Gascon component (eth/deth, ish, sh); the Mistralian minority is ignored here. In the classical norm o = /u/, ò = /ɔ/, so there are no vowel digraphs. Doubled ll, nn, mm, dd are geminates (/ll/ etc., one long sound in Languedocien, simplified elsewhere); assimilated clusters bt, gd, tl, tm, tn (/tt/, /ll/, /mm/, /nn/) are left as two graphemes. Interpunct sequences n·h, s·h (Gascon) cannot occur because · is not in the alphabet. Dialectal phoneme values vary a lot (Provençal, Gascon, Limousin, Auvergnat); grapheme boundaries do not. Context rules applied: tg only before e/i, tj before a/o/u, qu/gu only before e/i.

oromo-om.ambiguities: No native c+h, d+h, n+y, p+h, s+h clusters, so longest match is safe. Geminated digraphs are written by doubling the first element (pph, ddh, nny, cch, ssh — e.g. qopphaa'uu, baddhaadhe); longest match yields p + ph, which users may want to map to a long ph. The apostrophe is the glottal-stop letter (ja'a, ta'e) and is sometimes replaced by h or omitted.
oromo-om.notes: Qubee Latin orthography (official since 1991), very regular. Long vowels are written double (aa, ee, ii, oo, uu) and geminate consonants double (badaa vs baddaa) = one phoneme each, hence doubles = one. Single letters c = /tʃʼ/, x = /tʼ/, q = /kʼ/. Loan digraphs ts, zh (and letters p, v, z) are not native. Older texts used th for x and c/ch inconsistently.

ossetian-os.ambiguities: The labialised digraphs гу/ку/ху (+гъу/къу/хъу) are the main problem: longest match will merge г+у also when у is the vowel /u/ (e.g. word-final -гу, or гу before a consonant) – this is frequent, so users may prefer to drop the six labialised entries and treat у as a plain vowel. дз/дж are unambiguous in native words; in Russian loans ъ is a divider (объект) and д+з can be a cluster (rare). у before a vowel is /w/ (уа, уы) – single letter with two values, not a multigraph. ь occurs only in Russian loanwords (no palatalisation rule for Ossetian).
ossetian-os.notes: Standard (Iron) Ossetian Cyrillic; the corpus may also contain Digor texts, which use the same alphabet and digraphs with slightly different sound values (e.g. дз = [dz]). ӕ is a single letter /ɐ/. Doubled consonants spell geminates (ӕппӕт, ӕттӕ) = one long consonant. Iron phonologists (Abaev, Bagaev) list the labialised consonants gʷ kʷ xʷ qʷ kʼʷ ʁʷ as phonemes, which is why гу-type sequences are listed; this is a modelling decision. Decision: the labialised consonants (гу ку ху гъу къу хъу) are not listed, because longest-match tokenisation would merge every plain consonant+у sequence; they are counted as consonant + vowel.

pashto-ps.notes: Pashto Perso-Arabic script: every consonant phoneme, including the retroflexes ټ ډ ړ ڼ, ښ ږ and the affricates څ ځ, is one letter; no digraphs. The five yeh letters are single-letter vowel/diphthong graphemes: ي /i/, ې /e/, ی /aj/ (final) or /j/, ۍ /əj/, ئ /əj/ (2pl verb ending). و = /w/ /u/ /o/. Word-initial vowels are spelled ا + و/ی (او 'and' = /aw/, اوس /os/, ای-) – the epitran units او ای یو وو are such alif/vav sequences (وو = past copula /wu/ or و+و), i.e. letter-by-letter, not digraphs; excluded for the same reason as in Persian. Short vowels are unwritten. Doubled letters are two phonemes (وو, کوو).

persian-fa.notes: Perso-Arabic script, one letter = one phoneme for consonants; ا و ی are also the long-vowel letters /ɒː uː iː/ and و/ی the glides /v/ /j/; short vowels are unwritten; final ه spells /e/ (خانه). The ZWNJ (U+200C, listed as a modifier letter) only separates morphemes inside a word (می‌کنم, 2,347 corpus types) and never forms a grapheme – treat it as a word-internal boundary. Two sequences a researcher may wish to add by hand: (1) خوا in the closed set خواب خواهر خواستن خواندن خواهش خواجه خواه (277 corpus types, 'silent vav'): خو+ا = /xɒː/; and (2) word-initial ا+و / ا+ی spelling a bare initial vowel /u o/ /i e/ (او, ایران, اینجا) where the alif is only a carrier. Both are two-letter-for-one-phoneme-plus cases but are excluded here because the same strings are two phonemes elsewhere (خوب خود خوش; medial او = /ɒːv/). Doubled letters are two phonemes (تشکّر would need an unwritten shadda).

sindhi-sd.notes: Sindhi Perso-Arabic script (52 letters). Most aspirates and all implosives are single letters: ڀ /bʱ/, ٿ /tʰ/, ٺ /ʈʰ/, ڦ /pʰ/, ڌ /dʱ/, ڍ /ɖʱ/, ڇ /tʃʰ/, ک /kʰ/ (ڪ = /k/), ٻ ڏ ڄ ڳ implosives, ڃ ڱ ڻ nasals, ڙ /ɽ/, ٽ ڊ retroflexes; only /ɡʱ dʒʱ ɽʱ lʱ mʱ nʱ ɳʱ/ are written with ھ (Unicode L2/22-053; Shackle, Encyclopaedia Iranica). slovenian-sl.notes: Standard Slovene (Gaj's alphabet, 25 letters) has no digraphs: lj and nj are l+j, n+j (not the single phonemes of Croatian), and dž in loanwords (džez, džungla) is usually analysed as /d͡ʒ/ but is marginal. somali-so.ambiguities: d+h, k+h, s+h do not occur as clusters word-internally, so longest match is safe. Geminate dh is written dhdh in some texts (rare).
somali-so.notes: 1972 Somali Latin alphabet, highly phonemic. Long vowels are written double (aa, ee, ii, oo, uu) = one phoneme, and geminate consonants are written double (bb, dd, gg, ll, mm, nn, rr) = one long phoneme; hence doubles = one. c = /ʕ/, x = /ħ/, q = /q/ are single letters. p, v, z appear only in loans. Note Somali has a well-known vowel-harmony (ATR) distinction that is not written.

tagalog-tl.ambiguities: ng is unambiguous (n+g across a morpheme boundary is practically absent; ngg = ng+g as in tanggap, manggagawa). ts/sy/dy/ny are palatalised clusters rather than true single-phoneme digraphs for many analysts; longest match treats them as one unit, which is wrong in English loans spelled with ty/ts across a boundary (party, products, units) and in a few native words (kits). Doubled vowels are two syllables separated by a glottal stop (paano /pa.ʔa.no/, saan, maayos), so the general 'double = one grapheme' rule must NOT be applied to vowels in Tagalog.

tagalog-tl.notes: Standard 2014 KWF Ortograpiyang Pambansa: 20 native letters (abakada + ng) plus 8 borrowed letters (c f j ñ q v x z) used only in proper names and unassimilated loans. The corpus contains many unassimilated English/Spanish spellings (school, show, hello, sorry, quality, ch/sh/ll/rr/qu/ci/ce) which are not Tagalog graphemes and were not listed. Diphthongs ay/aw/iw/oy/uy are vowel + glide consonant (y, w) in Philippine phonology and are not listed. ñ is a single letter (only 2 corpus types). Only ng is beyond doubt; whether to keep ts/sy/dy/ny as digraphs is a the tool's authors decision (epitran uses ch, ny, ng, sy). Decision: the loan spellings ts, sy, dy, ny, ty, ly are treated as consonant + y/s sequences, not graphemes; only ng is merged.

urdu-ur.notes: Standard Urdu orthography (Perso-Arabic, Nastaliq). Besides the aspirate digraphs the script is letter-per-phoneme for consonants; short vowels are unwritten; ا و ی ے are the vowel letters (ے = /eː ɛː/ word-finally only), ہ final often spells /ɑ/ /ɛ/ (کہ, نہ). Word-initial vowels are spelled ا + و/ی (اور, ایک) and the 'silent vav' sequence خوا (خواب, خواتین, خواہش; 189 types) spells /xɑː/ – both excluded as in Persian. ئ and ؤ are hamza-carrier letters before/after vowels (آئی, کوئی, ہوئے).

uyghur-ug.notes: Uyghur Arabic alphabet (UEY, reformed 1983): 32 letters, fully phonemic for consonants and with eight dedicated vowel letters, so apart from the hamza-carrier convention it is one letter = one phoneme. ئ is listed as a modifier letter in alphabets.tsv; if the tool already treats a modifier+vowel as one unit, these eight entries are redundant but harmless. The epitran map for uyghur-ug contains exactly these eight units.

uzbek-uz.ambiguities: ng = n+g at suffix boundaries (dative -ga after n: o'rmonga, tonga) and in loans (kongress, ingliz); the pronunciation is [ŋɡ] so longest match gives one grapheme where there are two phonemes — a few percent of ng tokens. sh = s+h is written with an apostrophe (Is'hoq) so it is safe; ch is always the digraph. The modifier letter/apostrophe also serves as tutuq belgisi after other vowels and consonants (a'lo, san'at, ma'no, mas'ul): there it is not part of a grapheme and the tool should ignore a lone ʻ or ' that does not follow o or g. Where the mark after o is the glottal sign rather than the letter oʻ the two are indistinguishable in writing (rare). A number of corpus words lack the apostrophe altogether (togri, ornak, bula for toʻgʻri, oʻrnak, boʻla) and cannot be recovered.

Vietnamese words in the lexicon are monosyllables, so cross-morpheme boundary problems (t+h, n+g, n+h) do not arise.

vietnamese-vi.notes: Standard quốc ngữ. The pipeline keeps precomposed tone-marked vowels, so every vowel multigraph has five extra tone-marked spellings; the tone-bearing letter follows the modern rule (ia ua ưa: first letter; iê uô ươ yê: the second letter). ă â ê ô ơ ư đ are single letters; c/k/q are allographs of /k/; d = /z/ (north) is a single letter distinct from đ. Doubled vowels do not occur in native words (oo only in a few loans), hence doubles = n/a (a doubled vowel in a loan is one vowel); doubled consonants never occur.

volapuk-vo.ambiguities: No digraphs; adjacent vowels (ai, ei, oi in 'bai', 'dei') are separate syllables, not diphthongs. ä ö ü are single letters. Doubled letters essentially do not occur outside loan names.
volapuk-vo.notes: Volapük spelling (Schleyer 1879, de Jong 1931) is strictly one letter – one phoneme: c = /tʃ/, j = /ʃ/, x = /ks/, z = /ts/, y = /j/. Corpus is small (2.3k types).

voro-vro.ambiguities: None at the letter level. voro-vro.notes: Orthography like Estonian (South Estonian): one letter = one phoneme, doubled letters = long sound. waray-war.notes: Waray has three native vowels (a i u, plus e/o in Spanish loans); no vowel digraphs; ay/aw/oy/uy are vowel + glide. yoruba-yo.notes: Tone marks were stripped, so the three tones are not recoverable and the Nigerian alphabet of 25 letters is otherwise phonemic; ẹ /ɛ/, ọ /ɔ/, ṣ /ʃ/ are single letters; p = /k͡p/. Doubled vowels (dáadáa, òun) are two tone-bearing syllables/moras, so doubles = two. Benin Yoruba conventions (ɛ, ɔ) are not in the alphabet column. Vowel + n counts as a nasal-vowel grapheme only when no vowel letter follows (before a vowel the n is a consonant).

zazaki-diq.ambiguities: th, ph in English/Greek loans and names (the, with, sophia, philos) are not digraphs; lh (sulh, ilham) and sh (ishaq) are loans and clusters, not graphemes; ng is n+g (veng /veŋɡ/, reng). The aspiration digraphs appear in a small minority of types (kh 20, ph 18, th 36, çh 9 of 13,925) because most writers do not mark the contrast.
zazaki-diq.notes: No single standard: the corpus (Zazaki Wikipedia) mixes the Jacobson/Zaza Language Institute orthography (ê ı i û, dominant), Bedirxan-style spellings, and idiosyncratic ones (ý for ı in 35 types, ü in 151, é in 40, ö in 4). The listed digraphs follow the Northern Zaza alphabet description at zazaki.de; researchers wanting strict one-letter spelling may drop them. Letters ç ş ğ ê î û ü ö é ı are single graphemes; x = /x/, q = /q/, w = /w/, c = /dʒ/. Decision: the kh/ph/th/çh spellings of unaspirated stops are rare in the corpus (about 80 word types) and not used consistently, so they are not merged.

zulu-zu.ambiguities: Longest match works for the click series (ngc > nc > c, ngq > nq > q, ngx > nx > x) and for tsh > ts/sh. Problem cases: the sequence n+hl (e.g. in -ntlanzi type words) is written ntl in Xhosa but n+hl/ndl in Zulu, so hl stays correct; kl is always /kx/; ng before a vowel is /ŋɡ/ but ng before a vowel at a prefix boundary is the same unit; hh vs h+h never clashes. The prefix-boundary cases (umu-+ -ntu) do not create spurious digraphs because Zulu prefixes end in vowels. The Xhosa-only trigraphs nkc/nkq/nkx do not occur in Zulu spelling.

zulu-zu.notes: Vowel length and tone are never written, so no vowel multigraphs and effectively no doubled letters (hh is a digraph, not a doubled letter). Older texts wrote ɓ and plain b where current spelling has b and bh. Depressor nasals are not marked (mh, nh are Xhosa, not Zulu, conventions). Labialised sequences (bw, lw, kw, tw) and palatalised ty/dy are consonant + glide, not listed.
